title: Custom 'bind' Polyfill with 'new' Operator Support
concept: Currying, Prototype Chaining, and new.target Resolution
problemStatement: Implement `Function.prototype.myBind(thisArg, ...outerArgs)`. It must support partial application (currying), and when the bound function is invoked as a constructor using `new BoundFn()`, the provided `thisArg` MUST be ignored and a new instance inheriting from the original function's prototype must be created.
interviewTrap: 90% of candidates miss the `new` operator rule: when a bound function is called with `new`, the bound `thisArg` is completely ignored in favor of the newly instantiated object.

testCases.name: Standard bound invocation with curried arguments
testCases.testFn: function add(a, b) { return a + b; } const add10 = add.myBind(null, 10); return add10(20);

testCases.name: Maintains object this context
testCases.testFn: const user = { name: 'Alex' }; function getName() { return this.name; } return getName.myBind(user)();

testCases.name: Supports 'new' operator correctly overriding thisArg
testCases.testFn: function Point(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } const BoundPoint = Point.myBind({ x: 99 }, 5); const pt = new BoundPoint(10); return { x: pt.x, y: pt.y, isInstance: pt instanceof Point };

details.name: Standard bound invocation with curried arguments

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: A complete polyfill for `Function.prototype.myBind` must not only bind `this` and partially apply arguments (currying), but also support being used with the `new` operator. When a bound function is constructed (`new boundFn()`), the bound `this` must be IGNORED and a fresh instance of the original constructor must be created instead.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Check if called via `new`: `this instanceof bound` (or `new.target`).
If called via `new`, use `this` (the newly instantiated object); otherwise, use the originally supplied `boundThis`.
Inherit prototype chain: Set `bound.prototype = Object.create(targetFn.prototype)` so instances pass `instanceof targetFn` checks.
Execute `targetFn.apply(effectiveThis, allArgs)` and return result (handling constructor object returns).
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: ECMA-262 §10.4.1.1 specifies `[[Construct]]` on Bound Function Exotic Objects. When constructed via `new`, the bound function delegates to the original constructor's `[[Construct]]`, completely bypassing `[[BoundThis]]`. Our polyfill replicates this specification requirement faithfully.

complexity.time: O(1) creation; O(1) dispatch per call.
complexity.space: O(A) space for bound arguments array.

edgeCasesHandled: Constructor usage (`new boundFn()`) ignores `boundThis` and instantiates target prototype.
Partial application (currying) combines initial arguments with runtime arguments.
Instanceof operator works for both bound and original constructor.

specifications: ECMA-262 §10.4.1.1 [[Construct]] on Bound Function Exotic Objects
MDN Web Docs: Function.prototype.bind polyfill specification
verifiedRules: new operator overrides bound thisArg per ECMA-262 §10.4.1.1.
Prototype link must preserve instanceof operator validity.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: When a function returned by bind() is called with the 'new' operator, what happens to the bound this?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: When a bound function is invoked with `new` (`new boundFn()`), the originally bound `this` argument is completely IGNORED! Instead, a new object is created and its prototype is linked to the target constructor's prototype (`targetFn.prototype`). Any curried arguments passed to `bind()` are still prepended to the constructor invocation.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: The gold standard question for Function.prototype.bind polyfills (ECMA-262 §10.4.1.1).

interviewCrossQuestions.question: How does a bind polyfill detect if it was invoked via 'new' vs standard invocation?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: Inside the bound function wrapper, check `this instanceof boundFn` (or in modern JS, `new.target`). If `this instanceof boundFn` is true, the function was invoked as a constructor via `new`, so you use `this` (the newly allocated instance). Otherwise, you use the closed-over `boundThis`.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Tests understanding of constructor instantiation semantics and prototype chain checking.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: How do you ensure 'instanceof targetFn' still returns true for instances created from the bound function?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: You must establish a prototype chain between the bound function and the original target function. By setting `boundFn.prototype = Object.create(targetFn.prototype)`, any object constructed with `new boundFn()` inherits from `targetFn.prototype`, ensuring `instance instanceof targetFn` evaluates to true.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Tests precision in prototypal inheritance wiring.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: Can you re-bind a function that has already been bound with .bind()?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: No! Once a function is bound via `const b = fn.bind(objA)`, calling `b.bind(objB)` will NOT change `this`. The exotic bound function object wraps the original function and always forwards `objA` as `[[BoundThis]]`. However, secondary calls to `.bind()` can still curry additional arguments.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Tests awareness of the immutability of bound function context.

realWorldUseCases.description: Services pre-bind configuration dependencies or database handles at application startup, distributing clean parameterless action triggers to handlers.
Library authors bind constructors to ensure instances created without `new` still instantiate the correct prototype without breaking.
realWorldUseCases.codeSnippet: function Chart(config) { if (!(this instanceof Chart)) return new Chart(config); }

howToExplain.opening: A specification-compliant `bind` polyfill must handle two major responsibilities: partial application (currying) and constructor override behavior when invoked with the `new` operator.
keyPoints: bind returns an exotic function enclosing boundThis and prepended bound arguments.
When invoked normally, it dispatches targetFn.apply(boundThis, allArgs).
When invoked with new, boundThis is discarded in favor of the newly constructed this instance.
The prototype chain must link boundFn.prototype to Object.create(targetFn.prototype) to preserve instanceof checks.
howToExplain.closingImpression: The fact that the `new` operator overrides a bound `this` proves that constructor instantiation is the highest priority rule in JavaScript's call-site hierarchy.
analogies: Like a VIP pass: the bound this lets you into the club under your sponsor's name, but if you buy the club (new operator), your sponsor's name no longer matters — you own the room.

commonMistakes.why: Arrow functions cannot be constructed with new! Using an arrow function throws 'TypeError: bound is not a constructor' when someone executes new boundFn().
commonMistakes.correct: You must use a standard function declaration with prototype inheritance to support the new operator.

followUpDeepDive.question: What does ECMA-262 specify regarding the .length and .name properties of a bound function?
followUpDeepDive.answer: Per ECMA-262 §20.2.3.2, a bound function has a `.length` equal to `Math.max(0, target.length - boundArgs.length)` (representing remaining expected parameters). Its `.name` property is prefixed with 'bound ' (e.g. `'bound ' + target.name`).
